ingredients.name: Cuttlefish or squid, cleaned
ingredients.notes: ink sac removed (Sri Lankan cooking does not use the ink), cut into rings or bite-sized pieces, scored if thick

ingredients.name: Tamarind juice or paste
ingredients.notes: adjust to taste; lime juice can be used as a milder alternative

ingredients.name: Coconut milk
ingredients.notes: 1.25 cups, split between thin and thick stages

steps.instruction: Clean the cuttlefish thoroughly, removing the ink sac (Sri Lankan cooking traditionally does not use the ink). Cut into rings or bite-sized pieces. Rinse briefly with the turmeric in water, then drain well and pat dry.

Heat the coconut oil in a wok or large pan over high heat. When hot, add the mustard seeds, fenugreek, and fennel seeds, and let them sizzle and pop for a few seconds. Add the curry leaves and pandan leaf.
Add the onion, garlic, ginger, and green chillies. Stir-fry over high heat until the onion softens and starts to brown slightly, about 3-4 minutes.
Add the curry powder and chilli powder, and stir for about 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the chopped tomato and cook until it softens, about 2 minutes.

Add the tamarind, sugar, and the thinner half of the coconut milk. Bring to a simmer and let the gravy cook for 5-8 minutes, until it darkens slightly and the flavours meld. Taste and adjust the seasoning at this stage, before adding the cuttlefish.
Add the cuttlefish pieces to the gravy and stir gently to coat. Reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer for 5-7 minutes -- watch closely, as cuttlefish becomes tough and rubbery if overcooked.
Pour in the remaining thick coconut milk. Stir gently and simmer for a final 2-3 minutes to warm through and slightly thicken the gravy. Taste and adjust salt.
Serve hot with rice, string hoppers, pittu, or bread.

source_site: islandsmile.org, cross-checked against topsrilankanrecipe.com, theseafoodblog.com, and nekokichi.wordpress.com for technique consistency
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 6+ independent sources; strong agreement on cooking cuttlefish briefly to avoid toughness, and the absence of squid ink in Sri Lankan preparations
notes: Known as dallo, kiri atha, or simply cuttlefish/squid curry depending on the household and region; the same recipe applies interchangeably to squid and cuttlefish. The single most important technique point across all sources is to avoid overcooking the seafood -- cuttlefish and squid turn tough and rubbery very quickly, so they are typically added to an already-developed, well-seasoned gravy rather than simmered for a long time. Unlike most Western preparations, Sri Lankan cooks discard the ink sac entirely rather than using it for colour or flavour. This curry pairs particularly well with a starchy, less spicy side (rice, pittu, or string hoppers) to balance its tangy, spicy gravy.
